introduction: Today we celebrate the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ. Moses reminds Israel how God fed them with manna in the desert. Paul says that because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. In the Gospel, Jesus says, I am the living bread that came down from heaven; whoever eats this bread will live forever. In many places, a procession with the Blessed Sacrament follows Mass. Let us adore Christ, the bread of life.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, Christ gives us his flesh as the bread of life. Let us bring our prayers to the Father.
intentions: For the Church: that the Eucharist may make her one body, united in faith and love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For priests: that they may celebrate the Eucharist with reverence and joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who hunger, for bread or for God: that they may be fed. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are separated from the Eucharist: that Christ may draw them back to his table. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may adore Christ in the Blessed Sacrament and live because of him. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the living bread that came down from heaven. Help us to adore you in this sacrament, and to become one body in you. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: The living bread
reflection.body:
Moses asks the Israelites to remember their forty years in the desert. God let them be hungry and then fed them with manna, "that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of the LORD's mouth." God provided for them every day, and he "poured water for you out of the rock of flint."

In the Gospel, Jesus speaks of a bread greater than the manna: "I am the living bread which came down out of heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Yes, the bread which I will give for the life of the world is my flesh." His listeners are shocked: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?"

Jesus does not soften his words. He says them more strongly: "unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you don't have life in yourselves." And he promises: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day." The Eucharist is not a symbol only. It is Christ himself, given as food.

Jesus also describes the communion it creates: "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood lives in me, and I in him."

Paul draws out what this means for the Church: "Because there is one loaf of bread, we, who are many, are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf of bread." Receiving the Body of Christ makes us the Body of Christ. We cannot receive him and remain divided from one another.

If there is a Corpus Christi procession, take part. This week, spend some time in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament. And let your Communion lead to unity: make peace with someone from whom you are divided.
